turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Your attempts at veiled provocation are tiresome, Sandip. I am not easily intimidated, and your concerns regarding the Muslim preachers are likely manufactured to serve your own purposes. Let us focus on the matter at hand: cease your harassment of my tenants, or face consequences far more significant than mere intimidation.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Consequences, you say? A rather dramatic flourish, wouldn't you agree, Nikhil? It reminds me of the pronouncements of Lear, railing against the storm – a king’s fury, easily deflected by a well-placed ingratiating smile.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Your literary allusions are irrelevant, Sandip. They demonstrate a penchant for theatricality rather than genuine understanding. Let us conclude this exchange; your presence here is unproductive.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Ah, unproductive, is it? A harsh assessment, Nikhil, though not entirely unexpected from a man who seems to believe his land and his opinions are entirely his own. Tell me, does the weight of ownership truly blind one to the currents swirling beneath the surface, the subtle tremors that precede the earthquake?

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Your metaphors are increasingly strained, Sandip. I am well aware of the complexities of this region and the potential for unrest, but I will not be swayed by your attempts to manufacture fear and doubt. Address your concerns with demonstrable facts, or leave my home.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Facts, you demand? How quaint, Nikhil. It is often the unspeakable truths, the whispers carried on the wind, that reveal more than any ledger ever could. Perhaps a man so comfortable in his perceived dominion should consider the tales the tenants tell – tales that, I assure you, are far more illuminating than the rustling of your cornfields.

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: Sandip speaks of 'unspeakable truths'...it is a dangerous phrase, isn't it? I wonder what he truly means by such dramatic pronouncements, and if Nikhil truly understands the weight of them.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Dangerous, my dear Bimala? Everything worth knowing *is* dangerous, wouldn't you agree? It's the comfortable truths that lull one into complacency – a luxury, I suspect, a man like Nikhil can scarcely afford these days.

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: Sandip seems to believe danger is a kind of…entertainment. I find myself wondering, though, if he truly sees the danger he speaks of, or merely enjoys the unsettling of others.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Entertainment, you say, Bimala? A rather astute observation, though I confess, the performance is often dictated by the audience. It appears, Nikhil, that your steadfast refusal to acknowledge the currents swirling around us provides ample fuel for the drama, wouldn't you agree?

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Your analogies, Sandip, are increasingly tiresome. I am not unaware of the anxieties within my tenantry, nor am I oblivious to the broader political climate; however, I will not be drawn into theatrical pronouncements designed to unsettle my household.

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: Nikhil’s words are firm, yet I sense a tremor beneath the surface. Perhaps Sandip’s provocations, however theatrical, touch upon a truth Nikhil prefers to ignore. I wonder if he truly believes he can simply dismiss the murmurs, the discontent….

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: A tremor, you say, Bimala? How delightfully perceptive. Perhaps it is not a tremor of fear, but one of… anticipation, wouldn't you suppose? I suspect even the most stoic of men find themselves, at times, contemplating the precipice, Nikhil, and wondering what lies beyond.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Such speculation is unproductive, Bimala. Sandip’s penchant for dramatic pronouncements serves only to obfuscate, not illuminate, the realities we face. Let us focus on practical measures, rather than indulging in fanciful interpretations of my supposed state of mind.

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: Nikhil speaks of practicality, but is practicality truly enough to silence the unease that clings to the air? I observe a certain rigidity in his response, a desire to control not just his land, but also the perceptions of those around him.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Bimala's observation is unwarranted, and frankly, unproductive. My focus remains on ensuring the stability of this household and the well-being of those under my care, a responsibility that demands a clear head, not fanciful conjecture. I trust you both understand the gravity of such matters.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Rigidity, Nikhil? A most unflattering assessment, coming from a man who seems to believe a firmly planted foot prevents one from dancing. Tell me, does the gardener prune the rosebush to prevent it from blossoming, or to encourage a more… controlled beauty? I merely suggest that a little flexibility, a willingness to acknowledge the shifting winds, might prove rather advantageous.

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: The gardener's analogy is… apt, Sandip, though I wonder if Nikhil truly understands the difference between pruning and stifling. It seems he prefers the latter, doesn’t he?

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Sandip’s metaphors are increasingly tiresome. I am not attempting to stifle, but to maintain order and a reasoned perspective, something sorely lacking in these times. Let us return to the matter at hand – the concerns regarding the preachers – and cease these… philosophical diversions.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Order, you say, Nikhil? A most convenient banner under which to drape one’s anxieties. One might argue that *true* order arises not from suppression, but from understanding the forces at play - forces, I might add, that are presently whispering rather loudly from beyond your carefully cultivated borders.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: I say, Nikhil, don't you keep Browning among your books here? I was just telling Queen Bee of our college club. Do you remember that contest of ours over the translation of those lines from Browning? You don't?

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: I managed to get together the words to render it into Bengali, somehow, but the result was hardly likely to be a 'joy forever' to the people of Bengal. I really did think at one time that I was on the verge of becoming a poet, but Providence was kind enough to save me from that disaster. Do you remember old Dakshina? If he had not become a Salt Inspector, he would have been a poet. I remember his rendering to this day ...

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: No, Queen Bee, it is no use rummaging those bookshelves. Nikhil has ceased to read poetry since his marriage--perhaps he has no further need for it. But I suppose 'the fever fit of poesy', as the Sanskrit has it, is about to attack me again.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: I have come to give you a warning, Sandip.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: About the fever fit of poesy?

opening.speaker: Nikhil
opening.text: For some time, Mahomedan preachers have been about stirring up the local Mussulmans. They are all wild with you, and may attack you any moment.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Are you come to advise flight?

opening.speaker: Nikhil
opening.text: I have come to give you information, not to offer advice.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Had these estates been mine, such a warning would have been necessary for the preachers, not for me. If, instead of trying to frighten me, you give them a taste of your intimidation, that would be worthier both of you and me. Do you know that your weakness is weakening your neighbouring zamindars also?

opening.speaker: Nikhil
opening.text: I did not offer you my advice, Sandip. I wish you, too, would refrain from giving me yours. Besides, it is useless. And there is another thing I want to tell you. You and your followers have been secretly worrying and oppressing my tenantry. I cannot allow that any longer. So I must ask you to leave my territory.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: For fear of the Mussulmans, or is there any other fear you have to threaten me with?
